blocks.text: RELIC: Revealed Principles for Learning
Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning
heading_path: Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning

blocks.text: Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet* 1 Bui Dinh Pham * 1 Duong Quoc Chinh ** 1 Dao Van Tung** 1 Tran Cong Dao ** 2 Huynh Thi Thanh Binh 1
heading_path: Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning

blocks.text: Abstract

Multi-agent planning becomes substantially harder when agents must improve specialized decision-making skills while keeping their internal implementations private. This regime arises when agents are developed independently, expose different interfaces and capabilities, and must nevertheless coordinate without sharing executable policies. Prior research has largely assumed centralized optimization, shared policy access, or common skill representations, making it poorly suited to privacy-constrained cooperation. We introduce RELIC, a framework for learning interpretable and composable skills via revealed principles. Each agent refines its own programmatic skill through private LLM-guided search, while a trusted orchestrator evaluates proposed updates solely through team-level performance. Successful behaviors are not broadcast as code; instead, they are abstracted into portable principles that other agents can instantiate within their own interfaces and recombine with local strategies. This separates coordination from implementation sharing, enabling cross-agent transfer under heterogeneous skill signatures. RELIC thus introduces a new paradigm for privacy-preserving skill learning and coordination in multi-agent planning.
Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as search and synthesis engines for automated planning. Recent work has shown that LLMs can generate executable policies or planning programs, refine symbolic planning models, and support long-horizon decision making through reusable skills (Silver et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2023; Oswald *Co-first authors **Co-second authors 1Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, Vietnam2University of Sydney,

In parallel, a growing line of work studies skill discovery and skill libraries, where LLMs or offline data are used to acquire reusable behaviors that can later be retrieved, adapted, or composed (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Alzubi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). These directions have established that LLMs are effective at producing structured planning artifacts and reusable skills. However, most existing approaches assume that planning knowledge is improved in a centralized form: a shared planner, a common symbolic model, or a globally accessible skill repository. This assumption is limiting for multi-agent planning settings in which different agents expose different decision interfaces, specialize in different roles, and must still improve as a team. In such settings, the key challenge is not merely to optimize each skill independently, but to discovertransferable coordination structure: what aspects of a successful local policy can be abstracted, communicated, and re-instantiated by another agent with a different interface and role. We study multi-agent planning problems in which each agent is represented by its own programmatic decision skill, implemented as an interpretable function with an agentspecific signature. The agents must improve jointly as a team, yet candidate updates are evaluated only through overall team performance. This creates a coupled search problem: a local change should be retained only if it improves

blocks.text: coordination at the team level, while any useful behavioral structure should remain transferable across agents with different interfaces. We introduce RELIC (REvealed Principles forLearning InterpretableComposable Skills), a framework for learning in this setting. Each agent performs LLM-guided search over revisions of its own skill program, while a trusted orchestrator evaluates candidate updates under the current team and maintains the best joint solution. Rather than transferring successful skills directly as implementations, RELIC distills them intorevealed principles: compact descriptions of strategies or coordination patterns that can be re-instantiated under another agent’s local signature. This separates local program optimization from cross- 1

blocks.text: agent transfer, allowing coordination structure to be reused without requiring a common implementation space. Concretely, RELIC combines private per-agent program search, a shared public tree of revealed principles, and operators for principle instantiation and reflection. This perspective differs from prior multi-agent LLM systems that focus on communication protocols, centralized planning, or retrieval from pre-existing skill libraries (Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Our goal is instead to learn transferable coordination principles jointly with the underlying skills, under heterogeneous agent interfaces and team-level supervision. This makes RELIC well suited to teams of independently specialized agents that must develop interoperable behavior. This work makes three contributions. First, we formulate a new setting for multi-agent planning: learning interoperable programmatic skills under heterogeneous agent interfaces and team-level evaluation. Second, we propose RELIC, a framework that combines private skill search with principlemediated transfer to learn interpretable and composable behaviors. Third, across diverse multi-agent planning domains, we show that RELIC improves both team performance and cross-agent skill reuse over competitive baselines.

blocks.text: We study cooperative multi-agent planning with heterogeneous programmatic skills. A team consists of N agents indexed by i∈[N] . Each agent i receives local inputs from Xi, outputs actions in Ai, and acts through a decision skill πi :X i → Ai, implemented as an interpretable executable program with an agent-specific function signature. The input spaces Xi may differ across agents, reflecting heterogeneous roles and information access. We consider a stream of batches b= 1, . . . , B. blocks.text: LLM-Guided Program Tree Search
heading_path: Sydney, Australia. Correspondence to: Huynh Thi Thanh Binh

blocks.text: RELIC builds on LLM-guided program search methods such as MCTS-AHD (Zheng et al., 2025) and MOTIF (Kiet et al., 2026), which represent search directly in code space. For each agent i, we maintain a search tree Ti whose nodes are candidate skill programs. The root node contains a seed skill, and each child node is obtained by applying an LLM-guided editing operator to its parent program. Each node stores a candidate skill π, together with standard tree-search statistics such as visit count N(π) and value estimate Q(π). Node selection follows an upper-confidence criterion; for a child nodeπ ′ of parentπ, UCT(π′) =Q(π ′) +c s lnN(π) N(π ′) ,(3) where c >0 is an exploration constant. This representation is well suited to RELIC because each search state remains an interpretable executable skill, while LLM operators can revise code in structured ways rather than regenerate policies from scratch.

blocks.text: Revealed Principles and Public Tree
heading_path: Sydney, Australia. Correspondence to: Huynh Thi Thanh Binh

blocks.text: RELIC transfers behavior throughrevealed principles, i.e., short textual abstractions of successful skills. It maintains two principle memories: a local archive Arev i,b for each agent i, and a shared public tree Pb. Each public node p∈ Pb stores a principle text ρ(p), a type τ(p), a contributor κ(p), a visit countN(p), and a cumulative endorsementE(p). 3

Public-tree retrieval and endorsement.WhenBis invoked by agent i, RELIC selects a public principle contributed by another agent using Upub(p) = E(p) N(p) +cpub s lnP q∈Pb N(q) N(p) , κ(p)̸=i.(19) If a Bridge-derived revision that references p achieves positive gain∆ b >0, RELIC updates E(p)←E(p) + ∆ b, N(p)←N(p) + 1.(20) Principles with repeatedly positive downstream impact therefore become easier to retrieve, while low-endorsement leaf nodes are periodically pruned. Experiments
Baselines.We compare RELIC against six baselines.GS performs exhaustive grid search over handcrafted rolespecific heuristics for agents A, B, C.HHS(Cowling

et al., 2001) is a contextual selection hyper-heuristic over the same candidate set.CCEA(Potter & Jong, 2000) applies cooperative coevolution, with one species per agent and weighted mixtures of heuristic components as individuals.HAOS(Pei et al., 2024) uses a learned gate to switch between offline and online hyper-heuristic selectors.RL-ISis an RL-based hyper-heuristic, adapted from DRLH (Kallestad et al., 2023), that trains an instance-level policy for each agent to choose among candidate heuristics. We also compare toMOTIF(Kiet et al., 2026), the closest LLM-based baseline: although many methods search over code with LLMs, MOTIF is the only one we found that can optimize multiple functions with heterogeneous signatures.
Table 1 summarizes the main comparison. Among the base-

lines, all methods other than RELIC are trained in a centralized offline regime: GS, HHS, CCEA, and MOTIF operate on the full training set, while HAOS and RL-IS use batches but still revisit a fixed offline dataset over multiple epochs rather than adapting to a non-stationary stream. By contrast, RELIC refines skills in a decentralized manner at the agent level while handling streaming batches under centralized orchestration. blocks.text: Appendix: Supplementary Material
RELIC: Revealed Principles for Learning Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning
heading_path: RELIC: Revealed Principles for Learning Interpretable Composable Skills in Multi-Agent Planning

blocks.text: A. Related Works

We briefly review the most relevant research threads surrounding our setting, with particular emphasis on LLM-based heuristic construction, reusable skill learning, and decentralized cooperation. This discussion clarifies the gap addressed by RELIC: interoperable skill discovery across independently trained agents under limited information sharing.
A.1. LLMs for Automated Heuristic Design
heading_path: A.1. LLMs for Automated Heuristic Design

blocks.text: Recent work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can serve as powerful search operators forautomated heuristic design(AHD), where the goal is to discover high-quality algorithmic components with minimal human intervention. A representative line of work is EoH (Liu et al., 2024), which combines evolutionary search with LLM-based generation of both high-level heuristic ideas and executable code, demonstrating that natural-language “thoughts” can be treated as evolving search objects alongside programs. ReEvo (Ye et al., 2024) further develops this direction by framing LLMs as reflective hyper-heuristics, using iterative self-reflection and evolutionary improvement to generate stronger heuristics and meta-heuristics across optimization tasks. Moving beyond population-based evolution, MCTS-AHD (Zheng et al., 2025) replaces greedy population updates with Monte Carlo Tree Search, preserving a richer search history and enabling more comprehensive exploration of the heuristic space. More recent work expands the design space beyond a single heuristic. MOTIF (Kiet et al., 2026) formulates automated solver design as amulti-strategyoptimization problem, where multiple interdependent components are improved through a turn-based interactive framework between LLM agents. EoH-S (Liu et al., 2026) shifts the objective from discovering one universal heuristic to constructing acomplementary heuristic set, aiming for stronger robustness across heterogeneous instances and distributions. HiFo-Prompt (ChentongChen et al., 2026) introduces hindsight and foresight mechanisms to
heading_path: A.1. LLMs for Automated Heuristic Design

blocks.text: guide LLM-based AHD, explicitly controlling the exploration–exploitation trade-off while accumulating reusable design principles over time. Overall, these methods primarily focus on centralized heuristic or component search. In contrast, RELIC studiescooperative planningunder decomposition, where multiple agents improve private decision functions separately while exchanging only abstract principles through a shared public structure.
heading_path: A.1. LLMs for Automated Heuristic Design

blocks.text: A.2. LLMs for Planning Optimization

A related line of work uses LLMs forautomated planning and optimizationin domains such as routing, itinerary generation, urban operations, and robot task planning. One common paradigm is to use LLMs as an interface between natural-language requests and downstream optimization modules. For example, TTG (Ju et al., 2024) translates user requests into symbolic constraints and then invokes a mixed-integer optimization solver to produce guaranteed travel plans. ItiNera (Tang et al.,
similarly combines LLM-based request understanding with explicit spatial optimization for open-domain urban
heading_path: similarly combines LLM-based request understanding with explicit spatial optimization for open-domain urban

blocks.text: itinerary planning. At a broader systems level, UrbanLLM (Jiang et al., 2024) studies LLMs as decision-making agents for urban activity planning and management, covering planning problems with realistic operational structure and constraints. These works show that LLMs are useful not only for language understanding, but also for generating structured optimization inputs and coordinating solver-based planning pipelines. Another closely related direction focuses onrobotic planning, where LLMs are combined with symbolic actions, affordances, or motion feasibility constraints. SayCan (ichter et al., 2023) grounds language-model action selection using robot affordances, enabling long-horizon execution of high-level tasks on real robots. Inner Monologue (Huang et al., 2022) extends this idea by incorporating environment feedback and re-planning during execution. ProgPrompt (Singh et al., 2023) represents robot plans as executable program-like prompts, improving situated task planning under explicit action and object vocabularies. More recent systems push further toward hierarchical and embodied planning: DELTA (Liu et al., 2025) decomposes long-horizon robot tasks before invoking automated planners, while LLM-GROP (Zhang et al., 2025) integrates visual grounding with task-and-motion planning for mobile manipulation. Compared with these approaches, RELIC is not aimed at directly producing a single plan for one instance. Instead, it learns and improves reusableplanning decision functionsfor cooperative multi-agent optimization, with private local search and restricted information sharing through

blocks.text: B. Problems & Algorithms This appendix presents the six benchmark optimization problems considered in this work. They are organized into two families. The first family,multi-agent path planning, concerns teams of mobile agents that must coordinate their movements on a metric graph under limited travel budgets. These models are directly relevant to applications such as persistent monitoring, environmental reconnaissance, search-and-rescue, and field servicing. The second family,multi-agent scheduling, concerns decentralized dispatching over multiple resources or processing stages, where each agent controls a local decision rule while performance is evaluated through a global system-level objective. Such settings arise naturally in manufacturing, service operations, warehouse control, and heterogeneous human–robot teamwork. Throughout this appendix, the set of agents is denoted by K={A, B, C}. Each agent controls one local decision function. The resulting problems are cooperative: actions are selected locally, but the objective is defined at the team level.

blocks.text: B.1. Multi-Agent Path Planning

Each agent k∈ Kstarts from the depot and must execute a route whose total travel cost does not exceed a budgetB >0. The three problems differ in the reward structure associated with visiting nodes. The practical significance of this model lies in coordinated sensing and surveillance, where redundant scans are undesirable and spatially complementary coverage is essential. Multi-Agent Dynamic Servicing.This problem studies cooperative routing under stochastic, time-sensitive demand (Kirac et al., 2025). For each non-depot node i∈ V \ {0}, service requests arrive over discrete time according to a stochastic process with intensity parameterλ i. A realized requestρis characterized by: iρ ∈ V \ {0}(location), τ ρ ∈Z ≥0 (arrival time), wρ >0(service value), δ ρ ∈Z >0 (deadline horizon). A request is active over the time window t∈[τ ρ, τρ +δ ρ]. In the benchmark generator, request values are drawn from node-dependent exponential distributions and deadlines are sampled from a finite discrete range. A feasible team policy must jointly determine the routes of the agents and the requests to be served. Let zρ ∈ {0,1}indicate whether request ρ is served before expiration. If agent k arrives at node iρ during the active interval of request ρ, then that request may be served. Since at most one request is served per arrival event, the realized service variables must satisfy node-time capacity constraints induced by the selected routes. The objective is to maximize the expected total serviced value: max π E "X ρ wρzρ # , 10

where π= (π k)k∈K denotes a collection of decentralized causal policies, and the expectation is taken over the request-arrival process. Route feasibility must still hold for every agent: TkX t=1 ℓvk,t−1,vk,t ≤B,∀k∈ K. This formulation captures online fleet coordination in settings such as maintenance dispatch, emergency response, and on-demand field service, where requests are spatially distributed, stochastic, and perishable.
B.2. Multi-Agent Scheduling

The second family concerns decentralized scheduling under asynchronous decision epochs. Each agent controls a local resource and repeatedly chooses which available job or task to process next. The team objective depends on the global interaction of these local dispatching decisions through release times, due dates, processing times, skill heterogeneity, and precedence constraints. Multi-Agent Job Dispatch.This benchmark follows parallel-machine job dispatch under weighted tardiness objectives (Kacem et al., 2012). Consider a set of jobs J={1, . . . , N} and a set of identical parallel machines M={1,2,3}, with one machine controlled by each agent in K. Each job j∈ Jhas release time rj, processing time pj, due date dj, and weightω j ≥0. Each job must be assigned to exactly one machine and processed non-preemptively. Let xjm ∈ {0,1}indicate whether job j is assigned to machine m, let Sj be its start time, and let Cj be its completion time. The weighted tardiness of jobjis Tj = max{0, Cj −d j}. A standard mixed-integer formulation is min x,S,C,π X j∈J ωjTj subject to X m∈M xjm = 1,∀j∈ J, Sj ≥r j, C j =S j +p j,∀j∈ J, and disjunctive no-overlap constraints on each machine. For all distinct i, j∈ Jand all m∈ M, let πijm ∈ {0,1}indicate whether jobiprecedes jobjon machinem. Then Si +p i ≤S j +M(1−π ijm) +M(2−x im −x jm), Sj +p j ≤S i +M πijm +M(2−x im −x jm), whereMis a sufficiently large constant. The objective is therefore to minimize total weighted tardiness. From an operational viewpoint, this problem is solved online: whenever machine m becomes idle at time t, its controller

selects one released and unassigned job from the available pool A(t) ={j∈ J:r j ≤t, jnot yet assigned}. This corresponds to decentralized dispatching in deadline-sensitive production or service environments. 11

Multi-Agent Skilled Tasks.This benchmark follows heterogeneous task scheduling with category-dependent agent efficiency (Fırat & Hurkens, 2012). Let J={1, . . . , N} be the set of tasks and let C={1, . . . , S} be the set of skill categories. Each taskj∈ Jis associated with: rj (release time), c j ∈ C(category), pj >0(nominal processing requirement), v j >0(value), d j (deadline). Each agent k∈ Kpossesses a skill matrix entry αks >0 for category s∈ C. If task j is executed by agent k, then its effective processing time becomes epjk = pj αk,cj . Let xjk ∈ {0,1}indicate assignment of task j to agent k, let Sj and Cj denote its start and completion times, and let zj ∈ {0,1}indicate whether the task is completed on time. A natural formulation is max x,S,C,z,π X j∈J vjzj subject to X k∈K xjk ≤1,∀j∈ J, Sj ≥r j,∀j∈ J, Cj ≥S j +epjk −M(1−x jk ),∀j∈ J,∀k∈ K, Cj ≤d j +M(1−z j),∀j∈ J, together with no-overlap constraints on each agent. For all distincti, j∈ Jand allk∈ K, withπijk ∈ {0,1}, Si +epik ≤S j +M(1−π ijk ) +M(2−x ik −x jk ), Sj +epjk ≤S i +M πijk +M(2−x ik −x jk ). The objective is to maximize the total value of tasks completed no later than their deadlines. This formulation is particularly relevant to specialist teams, where the same task may be easy for one agent but difficult for another. Multi-Agent Flow Shop.This benchmark follows three-stage flow-shop scheduling under weighted completion objectives (Kyparisis & Koulamas, 2001). The benchmark is a three-stage flow shop. Let J={1, . . . , N} be the job set and let

S={1,2,3} be the ordered set of processing stages. Stage s∈ Sis controlled by one agent in K. Each job j∈ Jhas release time rj, stage-specific processing timesp j1, pj2, pj3, and weightω j ≥0. Every job must visit the stages in the fixed order 1→2→3. Let Sjs and Cjs denote the start and completion times of job j at stage s. The objective is to minimize the total weighted completion time at the final stage: min S,C,π X j∈J ωjCj3. 12

The formulation is subject to release-time and technological precedence constraints: Sj1 ≥r j, C js =S js +p js,∀j∈ J, s∈ S, Sj,s+1 ≥C js,∀j∈ J, s= 1,2. Machine-capacity constraints must hold at each stage. For all distinct i, j∈ Jand all s∈ S, let πijs ∈ {0,1}indicate whether jobiprecedes jobjon stages. Then Sis +p is ≤S js +M(1−π ijs), Sjs +p js ≤S is +M πijs. The objective thus penalizes late completion of high-weight jobs at the end of the production line. In decentralized online form, whenever stage s becomes available at time t, its controller selects a job from the current admissible buffer Bs(t) ={j∈ J:jobjhas completed stages−1,is ready att,and has not yet started stages}, with the convention that stage1 uses release times rj as readiness times. This benchmark therefore captures local dispatching inside a multistage production system with strict precedence structure and globally coupled performance.
Experimental Settings

Evaluation protocol.We evaluate all methods on the six benchmark problems described in the previous section. Each problem uses the same three-agent setup, with one local decision function per agent. For every problem, training consists of a stream of five batches with 10 instances per batch. The training size is smaller than the test size: the three path-planning problems are trained on instances with N= 40 nodes, the job-dispatch and skilled-task problems are trained on instances with N= 30 , and the flow-shop problem is trained on instances with N= 25 . Evaluation is conducted on two larger held-out test sets withN∈ {50,80}, each containing20instances. RELIC processes the training stream sequentially in batch order. In contrast, all non-LLM baselines are trained in a centralized regime. GS, HHS, and CCEA operate on the aggregated offline training set; HAOS and RL-IS retain the batch decomposition but still train offline over multiple passes through the full stream rather than adapting in a single pass. For the heuristic-based baselines, the candidate primitive set is the same handcrafted role-specific pool used throughout the repository. For MOTIF, we match the problem interfaces, seed initialization, and search budget to those of RELIC to ensure a fair comparison. RELIC configuration.Unless otherwise stated, all RELIC experiments use the default configuration in the released implementation. We use gpt-4o-mini as the underlying LLM backbone with sampling temperature 1.0. At each training

batch, every agent performs 10 private search iterations, yielding 5×3×10 = 150 private program-expansion steps per run. The private search tree uses maximum depth 8, replay size 2, and equal exploration constants for node, operator, and public-principle selection. Agent roles and function signatures.Across all benchmarks, the three agents follow the same high-level role decomposition. Agent A is a myopic local decision maker: it observes only its own state and the currently available options. Agent B is teammate-aware: it receives limited runtime information about other agents, such as current positions, busy times, or local states. Agent C is global-planning oriented: it receives a denser system-level representation, such as full remaining-value vectors, machine-load vectors, or pipeline state. This design creates heterogeneous skill signatures even within the same cooperative task. RELIC must therefore learn interoperable behavior across agents whose executable functions expose different arguments and information.
